hook: John von Neumann was born on December 28, 1903, in Budapest, Hungary, and earned a doctorate in mathematics from Pazmany Peter University in 1926 while also training as a chemical engineer in Zurich. He emigrated to the United States in 1930 and in 1933 became one of the founding professors of the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, working alongside Albert Einstein and Kurt Godel. During and after World War II he contributed to the Manhattan Project and to early computing efforts, and in 1945 he wrote the First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC, which described a computer that stores its program and data together in the same memory. That stored-program design, since called the von Neumann architecture, became the basis for the IAS machine he built at Princeton and for nearly all computers that followed. He continued advising the United States government on computing and nuclear policy until his death from cancer on February 8, 1957, in Washington, D.C.

quick_facts: Born December 28, 1903, in Budapest, Hungary, and died February 8, 1957, in Washington, D.C.
Earned his mathematics doctorate from Pazmany Peter University in Budapest in 1926.
Became a founding professor of the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton in 1933.
Wrote the 1945 First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC describing the stored-program computer design now called the von Neumann architecture.
Directed construction of the IAS machine at Princeton, one of the first stored-program computers.
Received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from President Eisenhower in 1956.

achievements.title: First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC (1945)
achievements.impact: Described a computer whose program and data share one memory, a design known as the von Neumann architecture that still underlies the hardware running today's AI systems.

achievements.title: The IAS machine
achievements.impact: Directed construction of a working stored-program computer at Princeton that served as a template for similar machines built at other institutions in the early 1950s.

achievements.title: Theory of Games and Economic Behavior (with Oskar Morgenstern, 1944)
achievements.impact: Founded mathematical game theory, later applied to strategic reasoning in artificial intelligence and multi-agent systems.

achievements.title: Manhattan Project computation
achievements.impact: Applied numerical methods and early automatic computing to implosion-lens calculations, driving wartime demand for faster computation.
